strengths: Novel and technically well-developed method: a differentiable Gauss-Seidel projection layer that exploits locality/sparsity of physical-validity constraints, combined with implicit differentiation for backpropagation, enabling constraint enforcement as a hard requirement rather than a soft penalty during both training and inference.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper provides convergence proofs for the linearized coupled system (Thm D.1), for the Gauss-Seidel sweep as coordinate descent on a strongly convex quadratic (Thm E.1), and for conjugate-gradient convergence of the backward adjoint system (Thm F.1), which is uncommon rigor for this type of applied ML paper.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six diverse benchmarks (CASP15, Test, PoseBusters, AF3-AB, dsDNA, RNA-Protein) spanning protein-protein, protein-ligand, protein-nucleic-acid complexes, with multiple structural metrics (LDDT variants, DockQ, L-RMSD) plus physical validity.

Demonstrates a compelling practical benefit: with only 2 denoising steps the method attains competitive accuracy versus 200-step baselines while guaranteeing validity, yielding ~10x wall-clock speedup, which is a meaningful systems-level contribution.
Useful ablation study (Sec. 5.5) isolating the separate contributions of GS projection at inference vs. finetuning with the differentiable module, clearly showing both components are necessary.
Good qualitative analyses (Figs. 1, 3, 4, 6) that visually substantiate the claimed reduction of steric clashes/distortions relative to baselines.
Thorough appendix with full constraint formulations, pseudocode for training/inference, and a clear reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The 'Physical Validity' evaluation metric is defined using essentially the same constraint set C(x) (steric clash, chirality, stereochemistry, planarity, etc.) that the Gauss-Seidel projection is explicitly optimizing to satisfy at inference. Because the projection enforces C(x)=0 by construction, the headline claim of '100% physical validity' is close to tautological rather than an independent empirical finding, and this should be discussed more critically (e.g., via held-out or alternative validity criteria not directly used in the projection).

Structural accuracy is not uniformly state-of-the-art: on several benchmarks (e.g., AF3-AB, dsDNA) Boltz-2 (a 200-step baseline) clearly outperforms the proposed 2-step method on LDDT metrics, and many reported gains over other few-step/200-step baselines are within one standard deviation, so claims of matching SOTA accuracy are only partially supported.

Scalability of the Gauss-Seidel projection is not deeply analyzed: the number of constraints m scales with system size and can reach ~13M for a single complex; the paper only reports wall-clock comparisons on CASP15 binned by atom count and does not report memory/compute cost trends for very large complexes or the backward CG solve's iteration counts in practice.

The physical constraint set itself is entirely adopted from Boltz-1-Steering (Wohlwend et al., 2024) without modification, so the core novelty is restricted to the projection/solver mechanism rather than any new characterization of physical validity.

Only one backbone model (Boltz-1) is finetuned and evaluated; despite claims of being a 'drop-in' module for arbitrary frameworks, no experiments demonstrate integration with other architectures (e.g., Protenix, AlphaFold3-style models) to support generality.

Baseline physical validity numbers are reported as exactly 0.00±0.00 in multiple settings (e.g., Boltz-1, Protenix on AF3-AB and RNA-Protein), which, while plausible, is not sanity-checked or discussed, raising a question about whether the validity criterion is unusually strict or whether some baseline outputs were not post-processed in a way comparable to typical usage.

Limitations section is very brief (single sentence) and does not discuss potential downsides such as sensitivity to the penalty coefficient α, behavior when constraints are contradictory/infeasible, or the added training cost (2 weeks on 8 H100s) relative to baselines.

No comparison against other plausible hard-constraint techniques mentioned in related work (e.g., manifold-based diffusion, ADMM-style projections) to justify why Gauss-Seidel is preferable beyond a qualitative convergence-speed comparison against gradient descent alone.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: current all-atom diffusion-based structure predictors frequently violate physical validity (steric clashes, chirality errors, etc.), and the paper proposes to treat validity as a hard constraint rather than a soft training/inference bias.

The differentiable Gauss-Seidel projection combined with implicit differentiation is a reasonable and well-engineered way to embed a large, sparse constraint-satisfaction problem into an end-to-end trainable pipeline, with convergence/optimality arguments provided in the appendix (Theorems D.1, E.1, F.1).

The method achieves 100% physical validity on all six benchmarks tested, in contrast to soft steering baselines (Boltz-1-Steering, Boltz-2) which still show non-trivial violation rates, and does so with only 2 denoising steps versus 200 for most baselines, yielding a reported ~10x wall-clock speedup.

Reasonably thorough empirical protocol: six benchmarks spanning protein complexes, protein-ligand, protein-DNA, and protein-RNA settings, plus an ablation study isolating the contributions of Gauss-Seidel projection vs. gradient-descent guidance vs. finetuning.
Good documentation of implementation details (GPU implementation via WARP, CG backward solve, hyperparameters) that aids reproducibility, along with pseudo-code for training/inference algorithms.
weaknesses: The claim that the method 'achieves the same structural accuracy as state-of-the-art 200-step diffusion baselines' is not well supported across all benchmarks: Table 2 (relegated to the appendix) shows the method trails Boltz-2 substantially on AF3-AB (0.79 vs 0.87 Complex LDDT), dsDNA (0.78 vs 0.94 Complex LDDT, 0.70 vs 0.89 DNA-Prot LDDT), and RNA-Protein (0.32 vs 0.88 RNA-Prot LDDT). This meaningfully undercuts the paper's central accuracy claim and appears to be downplayed by moving these results out of the main text.

The core algorithmic idea (constraint projection via Gauss-Seidel sweeps, akin to position-based dynamics from computer graphics) is largely adapted from prior physics-simulation literature; the main novelty is the integration into a biomolecular diffusion pipeline via implicit differentiation rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The physical validity constraints themselves are directly inherited from Boltz-1-Steering's energy terms, so the paper's contribution is primarily how the constraint is enforced (hard projection) rather than what is enforced, limiting the scope of the conceptual contribution.

Evaluation is built entirely on finetuning a single backbone (Boltz-1); there is no demonstration that the projection module generalizes to other architectures (e.g., AlphaFold3, Protenix, Boltz-2), leaving open whether the approach is broadly applicable or specific to this one pipeline.

Training cost (8 H100 GPUs for two weeks) is substantial, and no code/checkpoint release is mentioned, which combined with the complexity of the GPU-based Gauss-Seidel/CG implementation raises reproducibility concerns despite the algorithmic pseudo-code provided.
Runtime comparisons mix training hardware (H100) and evaluation hardware (A6000) without clear justification, and no variance/error bars are reported for the wall-clock speedup claims.

The ablation study is conducted on a single benchmark (CASP15) only, limiting confidence that the reported necessity of finetuning + Gauss-Seidel projection generalizes across the other five benchmarks.

Several reported LDDT/accuracy differences between the proposed method and baselines are within one standard deviation of each other (e.g., many Table 1 entries), raising questions about the statistical significance of the claimed 'competitive accuracy' results.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and technically grounded approach that elevates physical validity from a soft inference-time bias (as in prior steering methods) to a hard, differentiable constraint enforced during both training and inference via a Gauss-Seidel projection.

Solid theoretical foundation: the paper provides convergence proofs for the linearized Newton system (Thm D.1), for the Gauss-Seidel sweep as cyclic coordinate descent on a strongly convex quadratic (Thm E.1), and for conjugate-gradient convergence of the implicit-differentiation backward pass (Thm F.1), giving confidence that the module behaves as claimed.

Strong, broad empirical validation across six diverse benchmarks (CASP15, Test, PoseBusters, AF3-AB, dsDNA, RNA-Protein) spanning protein-protein, protein-ligand, protein-DNA and protein-RNA modeling, with consistent 100% physical validity and competitive-to-state-of-the-art LDDT/DockQ using only 2 denoising steps versus 200-step baselines.

Practically significant efficiency gains (~9-10x wall-clock speedup over 200-step baselines and 23-46x over steering-based methods) that could meaningfully improve usability of all-atom biomolecular predictors.

Careful ablation study (Table in Sec 5.5) isolating the contributions of GS-projection-as-post-processing vs. GS-projection-with-finetuning vs. gradient-descent guidance, clearly demonstrating that both the differentiable projection and the finetuning are necessary for the reported accuracy/validity trade-off.

Good reproducibility support: detailed forward/backward algorithms (Algorithms 1-4), explicit constraint formulations (Appendix G), GPU implementation details (WARP library, batching, CG solver), and a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The method is only instantiated and finetuned on a single backbone (Boltz-1); despite claims of being a 'drop-in' or 'plug-and-play' module for arbitrary biomolecular frameworks, no experiments demonstrate integration with a second backbone (e.g., Protenix or AlphaFold3-style models), leaving generality largely unverified.

On some benchmarks (e.g., AF3-AB and dsDNA in Table 2), the 200-step Boltz-2 baseline clearly outperforms the proposed 2-step method in raw LDDT (e.g., 0.87 vs 0.79 on AF3-AB), which somewhat undercuts the paper's framing that the accuracy gap to 200-step SOTA is 'largely closed'; a more calibrated discussion of this trade-off would strengthen the claims.

Physical validity is evaluated using exactly the same constraint set that the projection module is trained/inferred to satisfy, which risks circularity — 100% validity is close to guaranteed by construction rather than an independent confirmation of realism; validation against external or orthogonal structural-quality checks (e.g., MolProbity-style or knowledge-based potentials) would make the validity claims more convincing.

Limited analysis of the projection module's own scalability/overhead for very large complexes (constraint count m can reach ~13M for a single example); while runtime totals are reported, a breakdown of projection-only cost vs. denoising cost across atom-count bins would clarify how the method scales to larger assemblies.

The convergence/runtime ablation (Fig. 5) and the main ablation study (Sec. 5.5) are conducted on a single structure/benchmark (PDB 8X51 and CASP15, respectively) rather than across all six evaluation datasets, so the generality of these specific findings is not fully established.

Training the finetuned model requires substantial compute (8 H100 GPUs for two weeks), which, combined with reliance on Boltz-1 pretrained weights, may limit reproducibility for groups without comparable resources, despite the detailed pseudocode provided.
